title: Merging K Sorted Linked Lists

A binary tree where the parent node is always smaller than its children, giving O of log n extraction of the minimum

concept: Given an array of k sorted linked lists, merge all of them into one single sorted linked list and return its head.

solutions.label: Collect and Sort
solutions.summary: Gather all node values into a list, sort them, then build a new linked list from the sorted values.

solutions.label: Min-Heap Approach
solutions.summary: Use a priority queue of size k to always extract the smallest head among all lists, appending it to the result.

solutions.label: Divide and Conquer Merge
solutions.summary: Pair up lists and merge each pair repeatedly, halving the number of lists each round until one remains.

sections.diagram:

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an array containing k sorted linked lists. Each list is sorted in ascending order. Your task is to merge all of them into one single sorted linked list and return its head.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I receive an array of linked list heads, and each individual list is already sorted. A few clarifying questions: Can the array be empty, or can some of the lists be null?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the array could be empty, and individual lists can be null. Also, k can range from zero to ten thousand, and the total number of nodes across all lists can be up to one hundred thousand.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. Can node values be negative?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, values range from minus ten thousand to ten thousand.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me summarize. I have k sorted linked lists. I need to merge them into a single sorted linked list. I should handle empty arrays and null lists. For example, given lists one-four-seven, two-five-eight, and three-six-nine, the result would be one through nine in order.

sections.title: Collect and Sort
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Step1["Step 1: Collect All Values"]
        L1["1 → 4 → 7"] --> A["Array: [1,4,7,2,5,8,3,6,9]"]
        L2["2 → 5 → 8"] --> A
        L3["3 → 6 → 9"] --> A
    end
    subgraph Step2["Step 2: Sort the Array"]
        A --> S["Sorted: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]"]
    end
    subgraph Step3["Step 3: Build New List"]
        S --> R["1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 → 9"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is straightforward. I'll traverse every linked list, collect all node values into a single array, sort that array, and then build a new linked list from the sorted values.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the complexity of that approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let capital N be the total number of nodes. Collecting takes O of N. Sorting takes O of N log N. Building the list is O of N. So overall time is O of N log N, and space is O of N for the array.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works, but it doesn't use the fact that each list is already sorted. Can you do better?

sections.title: Min-Heap Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Init["Initialize Heap with Heads"]
        H["Min-Heap: [1, 2, 3]"]
    end
    subgraph Round1["Extract 1, push 4"]
        H1["Heap: [2, 3, 4]"]
        R1["Result: 1"]
    end
    subgraph Round2["Extract 2, push 5"]
        H2["Heap: [3, 4, 5]"]
        R2["Result: 1 → 2"]
    end
    subgraph Round3["Extract 3, push 6"]
        H3["Heap: [4, 5, 6]"]
        R3["Result: 1 → 2 → 3"]
    end
    Init --> Round1 --> Round2 --> Round3
    style H fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style H1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style H2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style H3 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since each list is sorted, I only need to compare the current head of each list to find the global minimum. A min-heap of size k is perfect for this. I insert the head of each list into the heap. Then I repeatedly extract the minimum, add it to my result, and push that node's next pointer into the heap.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's trace through our example. Lists are one-four-seven, two-five-eight, three-six-nine.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The heap starts with one, two, three. I extract one, push four. Heap becomes two, three, four. Extract two, push five. Extract three, push six. This continues until the heap is empty. Each extraction is O of log k, and I do it N times, so time is O of N log k. Space is O of k for the heap.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great improvement. Since k is usually much smaller than N, log k is better than log N. Is there an approach that uses even less space?

sections.title: Divide and Conquer Merge
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Round1["Round 1: Pair and Merge"]
        L1["1→4→7"] --- L2["2→5→8"]
        L3["3→6→9"]
        L1 --> M1["1→2→4→5→7→8"]
        L2 --> M1
        L3 --> M2["3→6→9 (unpaired)"]
    end
    subgraph Round2["Round 2: Merge Again"]
        M1 --> Final["1→2→3→4→5→6→7→8→9"]
        M2 --> Final
    end
    style M1 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style M2 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style Final fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can use divide and conquer, similar to merge sort. I pair up the k lists and merge each pair. This halves the number of lists each round. After log k rounds, only one list remains.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: With our three lists: round one merges list one and list two into one-two-four-five-seven-eight. List three has no pair. Round two merges those two remaining lists into the final sorted list.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each round processes all N nodes once, and there are log k rounds, so time is O of N log k, same as the heap. But space is only O of log k for the recursion stack, since we merge in place without extra data structures. This makes it the most space-efficient solution.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. The in-place merging is a real advantage when memory matters.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        BF["Collect & Sort\nO of N log N time\nO of N space"]
        HP["Min-Heap\nO of N log k time\nO of k space"]
        DC["Divide & Conquer\nO of N log k time\nO of log k space"]
    end
    BF -->|"leverage sorted property"| HP
    HP -->|"reduce space"| DC
    style BF fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style HP fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style DC fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's wrap up. We covered three approaches. The brute force collects and sorts everything in O of N log N. The heap approach uses a priority queue to get O of N log k time with O of k space. The divide and conquer merge matches the heap's time but reduces space to O of log k.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that since each list is already sorted, we only need to efficiently pick the smallest element among k candidates at each step. Both the heap and divide and conquer exploit this, but divide and conquer wins on space.
